name: Diego Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head buyer at Ridgeway Auto Parts Wholesale, out past the ring road. We stock brake pads, filters, batteries and belts for about 250 garages and parts shops. I'm in at 6:45, with a coffee and the printout of what sold yesterday, which I still ask for on paper. Then it's the phone: Mr. Ferreira at the brake plant, a battery importer in the port, a man in Germany who only speaks to me in the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that people trust my word, and I've done deals on a handshake for thirty years. I like finding the right part number for a garage that's stuck. What wears me out is the new system. The owner's son put in a screen that tells me what to order, and every morning I have to explain to a laptop why I'm doing it differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, a bit of relief. At work I'd say the new system is mostly noise and we should keep doing what pays. With my friends at the football club I'd say it's overrated, like most things sold with a slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it keeps my days the same, but my days aren't wonderful. I'm 58, on less than other buyers earn, with under a month of savings, and the owner's son wants his own man in my chair. I know four thousand part numbers by heart, and the new software knows them too, but it doesn't know which supplier lies about delivery dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. I'd keep running my accounts by phone and going to the supplier lunches I've always gone to. I'd ask Mei, my wife, to keep her shifts at the post office, because her pay is what carries the rent. I'd try to stretch the car another year, and keep looking at my pension statement every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, I suppose. I'm not excited and I'm not frightened of the software. It's the chair that bothers me, not the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the owner's son wants his own man in your chair. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The son is 34 and wants everything cheaper and faster, and he's read a lot of books about it. He thinks my way is slow. He's not wrong that I'm slow, but I'm accurate. Half the year I save him more than a screen does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is actually in the bank if something went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say less than 3,000 in the bank, if you add every account. Mei's hours at the post office were cut last spring, so we lost about 200 a month. I'd not say we're poor, but there's no cushion if the boiler goes.

say: I'd say the new system is mostly **noise** and we should keep doing what pays.
With friends I'd call it **overrated**, like most things sold with a slogan.
think: The owner's son wants **his own man** in my chair, hype or no hype.
The software knows part numbers but not which **supplier lies** about delivery dates.
do: Keep running accounts by **phone** and go to the usual supplier lunches.
Ask Mei to keep her **post office** shifts, since her pay carries the rent.
feel: **Fine, I suppose**; the chair worries me, not the machine.
S0.quote: I know four thousand part numbers by heart, and the new software knows them too, but it doesn't know which supplier lies about delivery dates.
fieldNote: His worry is the owner's son and **his chair**, not AI; the machine is a tool in a power struggle.
Thin money, with his wife's lost hours, keeps even this calm scenario from feeling safe.

steps.text: Keep running the 250 garage accounts by phone and handshake
Wait and see what the owner's son does with the chair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's another wave and we'll get through it like the last ones. At work I'd keep my mouth shut around the owner's son. To my wife I'd say we need to count what we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My whole value is that I remember things. The software remembers more and never takes a sick day, and nobody has ever asked me what I do when it's wrong. I think the buyers go first, because buying is the thing on the card. I'm at the front of the queue and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep doing what I've done and try not to be noticed. I'd attend the half-day training they'll ask me to do, and I'd sit through it, but I'm not going to enjoy it. I'd start looking at the pension rules to see if I could leave at 60 and bridge to the state age with part-time work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. It feels like the end of something. I'd go quiet at home, and Mei would tell me to stop sulking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours or pay were cut, what would go first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the Sunday family lunches out at the restaurant, which my daughter Ana would hate. I'd drop the cable, cancel the gym that I don't use, and I'd ask Lucas to pay a bit toward the car. I'd rather sell the second car than fall behind on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the junior, Dario, because he's got a baby on the way. I'd tell him to sit next to the screen and learn it. I'd tell him the old way is finished and I'm only still here because the owner trusts me. That trust has an expiry date.

say: I'd say it's **another wave** and we'll get through it like the last ones.
At work I'd stay quiet around the owner's **son**.
think: My value is remembering things, and the software remembers **more**, with no sick days.
Buying is on the card, so I'm at the **front of the queue**.
do: Sit through the half-day **training** without enjoying it.
Check the **pension rules** for leaving at 60 and bridging with part-time work.
Drop cable, the unused gym and the Sunday **restaurant lunches**.
feel: **Heavy**; it feels like the end of something.
S1.quote: My whole value is that I remember things. The software remembers more and never takes a sick day, and nobody has ever asked me what I do when it's wrong.
fieldNote: Resistant by habit and quietly sure he's **first in the queue**; his answer is to stay unnoticed.
Worries for the younger buyer with a baby, and admits the owner's trust has an expiry date.

steps.text: Keep buying by phone and stay out of the owner's son's way
Drop cable, the gym and the Sunday restaurant lunches
Check pension rules for leaving at 60 with part-time work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nothing at work, because the owner would hear it. I'd tell my friends I think it's a bubble, and I'd half believe it. Then I'd go home and look at the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not going to pretend I have a plan. I have a mortgage, a wife who sorts parcels, and a pension I can count on one hand. If a machine does all thinking work in two years, buying is gone. The parts counter and the delivery vans last until the robots come, three years later, and I'm not on those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing is to go and talk to the owner, man to man, about what happens to me. I'd ask for the longest notice I could get. Then I'd ask Mei's cousin about warehouse supervisor jobs at the freight depot, though I'd be starting low at 58. I'd stop all spending except food and the mortgage and hold on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid. Cold in the stomach, like the day my father's garage closed. I'd keep it in for a week and then it would come out as a row.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long could you hold on if the pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe six months of the mortgage if we stripped everything. Beyond that we'd have to sell the house or ask Lucas and Ana for help. I'd hate that. I told them I'd never be a burden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners, in the end. Not the machine, because the machine doesn't decide. I'd also blame the government for sitting on its hands while everyone shouted about it. But mostly I'd blame myself for never learning the thing.

say: I'd say nothing at work, tell friends it's a **bubble**, and half believe it.
Then I'd go home and look at the **numbers**.
think: I have **no plan**, only a mortgage, a wife who sorts parcels and a thin pension.
Buying goes on the **stated date**; the parts counter and vans last about three years longer.
do: Talk to the owner **man to man** and ask for the longest notice.
Ask about **supervisor jobs** at the freight depot, starting low at 58.
Stop all spending except food and the **mortgage**.
feel: **Afraid**, cold in the stomach, like the day my father's garage closed.
S2.quote: I'm not going to pretend I have a plan. I have a mortgage, a wife who sorts parcels, and a pension I can count on one hand.
fieldNote: Honest and blunt: he has **no real plan** and says so; his answer is to ask for notice and hold on.
Self-blame for never learning the tools shows the cost of his resistance.

steps.text: Stop all spending except food and the mortgage
Ask about warehouse supervisor jobs at the freight depot
Ask Lucas and Ana for help only if the house is at risk

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's close enough to plan for, and I'd say it at home. At work I'd say nothing new, but I'd watch the owner's face every morning. Online I don't speak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years I can do on stubbornness. I'd keep my head down, work until 63 and hope the owners don't need my chair before then. If they cut me at 60, I'm in trouble, because the pension is small and the state age is a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself harder to cut by doing the part the software can't, ringing suppliers about their real stock and late shipments. I'd teach Dario everything while I can, which makes me useful in a way a screen isn't. I'd put 150 a month aside, and Mei and I would work out the lowest bill we can live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A knot, but a lower one than the two-year picture. Time takes some of the sting out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year if you wanted to be harder to cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the doctor, the dentist and fix the car in the first year, while I've got a paycheck. I'd get a price on a smaller flat, and I'd see how much we'd have if we sold the house in year four. I'd keep my options open and not make any big moves until I see the owners' hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want ten years instead, or is five better for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five suits me better. I could retire at 63 and take a part-time job doing something quiet, like parts counter work at a small garage. With ten years I'd at least try to learn the tool, but with five I'm not sure it's worth it.

say: I'd say it's close enough to **plan for**, but only at home.
At work I'd say nothing new and **watch the owner's face**.
think: Five years I can do on **stubbornness**; the danger is being cut at 60.
The pension is small and the **state age** is far away.
do: Do the part software can't: ring suppliers about their **real stock** and late shipments.
Teach **Dario** everything I know, so I'm useful.
Put **150 a month** aside and work out our lowest living bill.
feel: **A knot**, but lower than in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: Five years I can do on stubbornness. I'd keep my head down, work until 63 and hope the owners don't need my chair before then.
fieldNote: Plans around **stubbornness and timing**, not learning; success means staying in the chair until 63.
Doubts that learning the tool is worth it at his age, which keeps him exposed.

steps.text: Keep my head down and work until 63
Put 150 a month aside and work out our lowest bill
Price a smaller flat and a part-time parts counter job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we've got time. I'd shrug at work and say it's a long way off. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm gone before it matters, and that's a strange thing to feel guilty about. My son the mechanic still has to live in it. I'd be 68, but I'd be retired at 65, and I'd just hope the pension covers the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and pay down the mortgage as fast as I can, 250 a month. I'd stay out of the new tools unless the owner forces them. I'd talk to Lucas about learning the part of auto work that needs the thinking, diagnostics and ordering, so he's covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. There's a long road and I won't be on the worst part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son Lucas about his own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lucas to watch what the car makers do, and to get a second skill, like fleet maintenance or electric cars. I'd also say don't borrow for a big shop. A mechanic's hands last longer than a buyer's head, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a decent retirement look like for you and your wife, Mei?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have a little. If I could clear the mortgage by 65, we'd have the pension and Mei's part-time at the post office. It's not rich, but we'd sleep. I'd take sleep over rich at this point.

say: I'd say good, **we've got time**, and shrug it off at work.
I'd say nothing online, as usual.
think: Ten years means I'm **gone before it matters**, which feels oddly guilty.
My son the mechanic still has to live in the **aftermath**.
do: Pay down the mortgage by **250 a month**.
Stay out of the new tools unless the owner forces them.
Push Lucas toward **diagnostics and ordering**, and a second skill.
feel: **Calm-ish**; I won't be on the worst part of the road.
S4.quote: Ten years means I'm gone before it matters, and that's a strange thing to feel guilty about. My son the mechanic still has to live in it.
fieldNote: Safe for himself but guilty about his **son's future**; long runway shifts the worry to family.
Still avoids the tools, so he relies on timing, not skill.

steps.text: Pay down the mortgage by 250 a month to clear it by 65
Push Lucas toward diagnostics work and a second skill
Keep buying by phone and stay out of the new tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time, a house I still owe on, and nothing in the bank. What would help is a long notice period, a fair payout and a pension that doesn't depend on me working until 65. And maybe somebody to show me the tools without making me feel stupid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against change. I'm against being told to change by people who won't be around to see what it costs. I'd have learned the tools if somebody had asked me nicely a few years ago, instead of putting a screen on my desk.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change. I'm against being told to change by people who won't be around to see what it costs.
portrait: Diego Chen, 58, is the **head buyer** at an auto parts wholesaler serving about 250 garages and shops.
He's resistant to technology, never uses AI, and has **under a month saved**, with his wife's hours cut.
He's pragmatic, avoids politics, and runs on **handshake trust** with suppliers.
His mood goes from uneasy to **alarmed** when AI comes fast, and eases when retirement lies before it.
He'd cut spending, **keep his head down** and use timing, not learning, to get to 63.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, with a mortgage and nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: A long **notice period**, a fair payout, a pension that doesn't need work to 65, and gentle help with the tools.
